title: Quilts in centimeters, on A4
summary: The quilt planner and every block can now be measured in centimeters: a true metric pattern with a 0.75 cm seam, cuts on half-centimeter marks, fabric in meters and PDFs on A4. English pages open in inches and the others in centimeters, and either can switch.

body.text: Every quilt in the [quilt planner](/quilts/) and every block in the [block library](/blocks/) now offers inches or centimeters. It's a pattern written in metric, not inches converted: every number is one a metric ruler cuts.
How a metric pattern is worked out

The seam allowance is 0.75 cm, and everything that follows from it is three times its quarter-inch figure, so a metric block goes together just as an imperial one does. Squares and strips are cut 1.5 cm larger than they finish, and triangles start from squares 2.6 or 3.75 cm larger, rounded up to the next half centimeter. Fabric is bought in tenths of a meter, binding strips are 6.5 cm wide, and the PDF patterns print on A4 with a 3 cm square to check the templates against.

Switching a quilt to centimeters picks the nearest size at which its blocks' squares land on the ruler, so a 9" [Snowball and Nine Patch](/quilts/snowball-and-nine-patch/) becomes 22.5 cm, with 7.5 cm squares, and a 12" [Ohio Star](/blocks/ohio-star/) becomes 30 cm. English pages open in inches and every other language in centimeters, and a shared link keeps the units it was made in.

items.caption: Snowball and Nine Patch at 22.5 cm
A star sampler at 30 cm, with 5 cm sashing
Trip Around the World at 35 cm

title: A printable pattern for the whole quilt
summary: The quilt planner now downloads one PDF pattern for the whole quilt, however many blocks it's made of: the picture, fabric to buy, every cut, each block's piecing, how the top goes together, quilting, binding and templates.

body.text: The [quilt planner](/quilts/) now downloads a PDF pattern for the whole quilt, however many blocks it's made of. It's one reference to print and keep beside the sewing machine.

First, the quilt exactly as you designed it, prints and quilting included, with its size and how many of each block it takes. Then the fabric to buy for each color, with backing, binding and batting, and the cutting list for the whole top, grouped by color. Each kind of block follows, drawn in your colors, with how many to make and how to piece it. Last come the steps that put the top together, row by row with any sashing and border, then layering, quilting and binding, and what the finished quilt weighs.

A quilt of one or two blocks is named for them, like [Snowball and Nine Patch](/quilts/snowball-and-nine-patch/). One with more is a sampler, like the [star sampler](/quilts/star-sampler/), and its pattern lists every block it uses. Shapes that can't be cut with a ruler, such as curves, print at true size at the end, each named for its block. Like the patterns in the [block library](/blocks/), it comes in all seven of the site's languages.

title: Plan a whole quilt: prints, quilting, a cut map and its weight
summary: A new quilt planner lays classic block pairings out as a whole quilt, mixes in scrappy prints, draws stippling and other quilting you can turn on and off, prints a picture cut list, and weighs the finished quilt. Patterns can now be saved as favorites, colors and all.

body.text: The [quilt planner](/quilts/) takes the blocks from the [block library](/blocks/) and lays them out as a whole quilt. Start from a classic pairing, then change anything: the blocks, the colors, the layout, the prints and the quilting.

items.caption: Snowball and Nine Patch, whose dark corners join into chains
Charm squares up close: gingham, dots, florals and plain cotton
Meandering across an Ohio Star and a plain square
Churn Dash with more prints, stippled
Log Cabin turned a different way in each quarter

body.text: Every block in a quilt shares one palette: a block's first fabric takes the first color, its second the second, and so on. That's what lets two blocks join across their seams, as the dark corners of [Snowball and Nine Patch](/quilts/snowball-and-nine-patch/) run into chains. Repeat one block, alternate two (a plain square is one of the choices, as in [Ohio Star and plain squares](/quilts/ohio-star-and-plain/)), or make a sampler of up to twelve, like the [star sampler](/quilts/star-sampler/). Any block's page now links to the planner with that block in its colors.

Real quilts are rarely one fabric per color. Print noise swaps some fabrics for near shades and prints of the same color: gingham, plaid, dots, small and large florals, stripes and linen. Turn on scrappy and every piece takes any of the colors, as in [charm squares](/quilts/charm-squares/). Six scrap baskets, one for each season, a monochrome and every blue, are a quick place to begin, on the planner and on every block's page, and reshuffle deals the scraps out again.
Quilting you can turn on and off

Choose stippling, meandering, crosshatching, an outline a quarter inch inside each piece, or stitching in the ditch, and switch the lines on or off to see the quilt with and without them. Stippling and meandering are drawn as one continuous line that never crosses itself, the way they're sewn.

Under the quilt is a cut map: every piece the whole quilt needs, drawn to one scale in its own color, with how many to cut. Squares to be cut on the diagonal show the cut. Print it and tick off each line as you go.

The planner weighs the finished quilt, layer by layer: the top with its seams, the backing, the batting, the binding and the quilting thread, with a choice of cotton or polyester batting. It also says how much thread the quilting takes. The fabric and batting weights it uses are listed in the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/).

A heart on the quilt planner, every block and every knitting and crochet stitch saves the design to your favorites, colors and all. They show at the top of the [blocks](/blocks/), [quilts](/quilts/), [knitting](/knitting/), [crochet](/crochet/) and [patterns](/patterns/) pages, and open just as you left them. They're kept in this browser only.

title: Thirty-three new quilt blocks
summary: The quilt block library nearly doubles, from 39 blocks to 72: four more Advanced blocks, new stars, curves, appliqué and picture blocks, and classic designs in strips, squares and triangles.

body.text: The [quilt block library](/blocks/) grows from 39 blocks to 72. Every new block comes with its cutting list, piecing steps and yardage at any block size, with printable templates for the pieces that need them.

items.caption: Lone Star, every point sewn from nine diamonds
Storm at Sea, nine blocks side by side
Spider Web, with diamonds where the corners meet
Orange Peel, where the peels link into circles
A row of Schoolhouses with sashing
Card Trick, four cards in a ring

body.text: [Pineapple](/blocks/pineapple/) turns its logs 45 degrees with every round. [Storm at Sea](/blocks/storm-at-sea/) combines three kinds of unit, each with pieces set on point. [New York Beauty](/blocks/new-york-beauty/) sets an arc of seven sharp points around a quarter circle, and [Lone Star](/blocks/lone-star/) builds each of its eight points from nine small diamonds.

[Rising Star](/blocks/rising-star/) sets a small star inside a large one, [Card Trick](/blocks/card-trick/) seems to lay four cards over one another, and [Spider Web](/blocks/spider-web/) sews eight wedges from strips. For curves and appliqué there are [Orange Peel](/blocks/orange-peel/), [Grandmother's Fan](/blocks/grandmothers-fan/), [Bull's Eye](/blocks/bulls-eye/), [Tulip](/blocks/tulip/), [Butterfly](/blocks/butterfly/), [Heart](/blocks/heart/) and [Tumbling Blocks](/blocks/tumbling-blocks/), and for pictures, [Schoolhouse](/blocks/schoolhouse/) and [Sailboat](/blocks/sailboat/).

The rest build on familiar shapes. In strips and squares: [Half Log Cabin](/blocks/half-log-cabin/), [Chimneys and Cornerstones](/blocks/chimneys-and-cornerstones/), [Chinese Coins](/blocks/chinese-coins/), [Bars](/blocks/bars/), [Center Diamond](/blocks/center-diamond/), [Roman Stripe](/blocks/roman-stripe/), [Spools](/blocks/spools/), [Attic Windows](/blocks/attic-windows/) and [Tumbler](/blocks/tumbler/). In triangles: [Economy Block](/blocks/economy-block/), [Snowball](/blocks/snowball/), [Birds in the Air](/blocks/birds-in-the-air/), [Lady of the Lake](/blocks/lady-of-the-lake/), [Delectable Mountains](/blocks/delectable-mountains/), [Wild Goose Chase](/blocks/wild-goose-chase/), [Thousand Pyramids](/blocks/thousand-pyramids/) and [Zigzag](/blocks/zigzag/).
Piecing steps now list each size of unit on its own, so a block that mixes large and small units, like [Anvil](/blocks/anvil/), trims each to its own size.

title: Cables, lace, puffs and clusters
summary: Knitting gains cables and lace, from a rope cable to Feather and Fan, and crochet gains puff and cluster stitches. Every knit and crochet swatch is redrawn to look like the fabric.

body.text: The stitch pattern makers now go past knit, purl and the basic crochet stitches. In knitting, [Rope Cable](/knitting/rope-cable/) crosses four stitches every fourth row between purl columns, [Horseshoe Cable](/knitting/horseshoe-cable/) crosses one cable to the back and one to the front so they curve apart, and [Feather and Fan](/knitting/feather-and-fan/), also called Old Shale, uses decreases and yarn overs to pull the fabric into scallops. In crochet, [Puff Stitch](/crochet/puff-stitch/) sets soft puffs into the spaces of the row below, and [Cluster Stitch](/crochet/cluster-stitch/) closes three double crochets into one top. Each has its chart, row-by-row instructions written from that chart, a yarn estimate and a complete square pattern, in all seven languages.

items.caption: Rope Cable, crossed every fourth row
Feather and Fan, pulled into scallops
Puff Stitch, set into the spaces below

body.text: New symbols, written out in full

Charts gain the standard symbols: a circle for a yarn over, slanted lines for k2tog and ssk, crossed lines for a cable, a wide oval for a puff and a fan for a cluster. The written rows name each one the way patterns do, as C4F or yo, k2tog, and the abbreviations explain how to work any the stitch uses. The tests follow each written row back into stitches, at every width and gauge, and check that it matches the chart and keeps the stitch count.

The [knitting stitch](/knitting/) pictures are redrawn the way the [crochet](/crochet/) ones were: knit stitches as Vs, purls as bumps lying across, yarn overs as holes, decreases leaning their way and cables as bands crossing over each other. Each stitch on the knitting and crochet pages takes its own yarn color.

title: Mariner's Compass, Snail's Trail and more advanced patterns
summary: Three new quilt blocks, among them the first two marked Advanced, a diamond brocade for knitters, and three new crochet colorwork charts: an eight-point star, houndstooth and argyle.

body.text: This update adds patterns for when the basics feel familiar. In quilting, [Mariner's Compass](/blocks/mariners-compass/) sets sixteen points in three lengths around a center circle, and [Snail's Trail](/blocks/snails-trail/) turns four rings of triangles around a small four-patch so dark and light spirals curl out from the middle. Both are marked Advanced, a new level. [Kaleidoscope](/blocks/kaleidoscope/) joins them at Intermediate: eight wedges and four corner triangles, whose corners form circles when blocks are set side by side. Each comes with its cutting list, printable templates and yardage, at any size.

items.caption: Snail's Trail, nine blocks side by side
Kaleidoscope, where the corners meet in circles
An eight-point star in tapestry crochet
Houndstooth, a color change every few stitches

body.text: [Diamond brocade](/knitting/diamond-brocade/) is the first Intermediate knitting stitch: lines of purl stitches climb and fall across stockinette to outline a lattice of diamonds, on a multiple of 8 stitches plus 1. In [crochet colorwork](/crochet/colorwork/), the [eight-point star](/crochet/colorwork/eight-point-star/) uses four colors in tapestry crochet, [houndstooth](/crochet/colorwork/houndstooth/) changes color every few stitches across every row, and [argyle](/crochet/colorwork/argyle/) is a corner-to-corner chart with an overcheck through its diamonds. The houndstooth is charted the way the cloth is woven, as a 2/2 twill with four dark and four light threads each way.
Crochet swatches that look like crochet

The [crochet stitch](/crochet/) pictures are redrawn. Each stitch now shows its braid of top loops and a post as tall as the stitch, so single, half double and double crochet no longer look alike: a half double shows its third loop, a double the yarn over wrapped across its post, back loop rib the ridges its front loops leave, and mesh and moss stitch the holes under their chains. The stitches on the crochet page each take their own yarn color, too.

title: Weaving drafts: threading, tie-up, treadling and the cloth they make
summary: A new weaving drafter turns a weave structure into the full draft a weaver reads at the loom, with 26 traditional drafts to start from, from bird's eye and goose eye to monk's belt and houndstooth.

body.text: The new [weaving drafter](/weaving/) draws handweaving drafts: the threading across the top, the tie-up at the corner, the treadling down the side and the drawdown, the cloth they make. Pick a structure, from [plain weave](/weaving/plain/) and [twill](/weaving/twill/) to [point twill](/weaving/point-twill/), [overshot](/weaving/overshot/), [huck](/weaving/huck/), [M's and O's](/weaving/ms-and-os/) and [summer and winter](/weaving/summer-and-winter/), choose 4, 8 or 16 shafts where the structure allows, and stripe the warp and weft in your own colors. Download the cloth as a seamless SVG or PNG, or a PDF of the full draft to take to the loom.

items.caption: Goose eye: a point twill woven as drawn in
Houndstooth: a 2/2 twill, four dark and four light
An overshot diamond on four blocks
Huck lace, warp and weft floats on plain weave
Log cabin, plain weave in alternating colors

body.text: Each square of the drawdown is one crossing. It shows the warp where the shaft that end is threaded on is tied to the treadle for that pick, and the weft where it isn't. Filled tie-up squares are shafts that rise, as on a jack loom; on a counterbalance or countermarch loom, tie the empty ones. Overshot and summer and winter leave their tabby picks out of the drawdown, as drafts usually do, and the steps say which shafts to raise for them. Each draft also gives its longest float, so you can see at a glance whether the cloth will hold together.

Below the builder sit 26 traditional drafts and cloths, among them bird's eye, goose eye, dornik, crowfoot, monk's belt, huckaback, Bronson lace, houndstooth, glen check, log cabin and gingham. Each opens the builder with its threading, treadling and colors, ready to change. They are drawn for this site from the structures in G. H. Oelsner's A Handbook of Weaves (1915) and William Watson's Textile Design and Colour, both public domain, and listed on the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/) page. The tests check that every structure repeats seamlessly, every draft uses each of its shafts and treadles, and no float runs past fifteen threads.

title: Kolam, drawn around a grid of dots
summary: A new maker draws kolam around a grid of dots as a seamless repeat: a sikku kolam's single looping line, a pulli kolam's joined dots or a kambi kolam's closed lines, on a square, diamond or hexagonal grid.

body.text: The new [kolam maker](/kolam/) draws kolam around a grid of dots, called pulli, as a seamless repeat. Choose a [sikku kolam](/kolam/sikku/), where one line loops around every dot, a [pulli kolam](/kolam/pulli/), where curved petals join the dots, or a [kambi kolam](/kolam/kambi/), where closed lines run around dots and groups of dots without crossing. Pick a square, diamond or hexagonal grid, a single or double line and your colors, then download SVG, PNG or a printable PDF.

items.caption: A symmetric sikku kolam on a square grid of 81 dots
A sikku kolam on the diamond grid
Seeded random on a hexagonal grid, in a double line
A pulli kolam, its dots joined by petals
A seeded kambi kolam, its closed lines in two colors
A finer seeded sikku, 13 dots across

body.text: Each dot sits in its own square, and at each side of that square the line either crosses over to the neighbor or turns back around its own dot. Neighbors share that choice, so the squares always match: on the square grid there are sixteen such tiles. A sikku starts with a ring around every dot and opens rings into each other one at a time, keeping an opening only when it joins two lines into one, so it always ends as a single closed line that passes between every pair of neighbors. The maker's tests check that for every grid, size and seed.

With the symmetric rule each repeat holds one finished kolam, turned about its center: a quarter turn on the square grid, the two diagonals on the diamond grid and a half turn on the hexagonal one. Its line stays inside the repeat, so repeats sit side by side on an unbroken grid of dots. With seeded random the line runs across the repeat's edges and comes back in on the other side, so the whole surface is woven from one line. Change the seed for another; the maker remembers your last seed in this browser.

Kolam is drawn by hand across Tamil Nadu and South India, often at the entrance to a home, and for many who draw it, it has religious as well as ornamental significance. This maker borrows the dot grid and the rules of the line, not the practice, and it makes no claim about what any particular kolam means. The tile method follows Saty Raghavachary's Tile-based kolam patterns (SIGGRAPH 2004), and the rules for a sikku follow Venkatraman Gopalan's study of square-tile sikku kolams; both are listed in the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/).

title: Turing patterns that grow into seamless repeats
summary: A new maker grows spots, stripes, labyrinths and coral from the Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion model, on a grid whose edges wrap around, so every repeat is seamless.

body.text: The new [Turing pattern maker](/turing-patterns/) runs a reaction-diffusion simulation and draws what grows: [spots](/turing-patterns/spots/), [mitosis](/turing-patterns/mitosis/), [coral](/turing-patterns/coral/), [labyrinths](/turing-patterns/labyrinth/), stripes, worms, holes and bubbles. Set the grid, the number of steps and which way the chemicals spread, choose filled shapes, outlines or two bands, then download a seamless repeat or a printable PDF.

items.caption: A labyrinth stretched across into stripes

body.text: Each cell trades chemicals only with its eight neighbors, and the grid's left edge counts as the right edge's neighbor, as the top does the bottom's, so the pattern grows on the surface of a doughnut. The edge of each shape is traced where the second chemical crosses the level you pick, then smoothed into curves whose bends carry over the join, so a shape cut by the edge of the repeat comes back in on the other side exactly where it left. The start is seeded and the arithmetic is fixed, so the same settings grow the same pattern every time.

In 1993 John Pearson ran this model, the Gray-Scott model, across a wide range of feed and kill rates and mapped what each region grows ([Science 261](https://arxiv.org/abs/patt-sol/9304003)). Each preset is a pair from one of those regions. The mitosis and coral pairs, and the simulation step itself, follow [Karl Sims' tutorial](https://www.karlsims.com/rd.html). Both are credited on the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/) page.

title: Chinese lattice, in thick bars that repeat
summary: A new maker draws Chinese window lattice on six frameworks, from square fret to cracked ice, with frames nested in the openings and a repeat that always meets its neighbors.

body.text: The new [Chinese lattice maker](/chinese-lattice/) draws window-grille lattice in thick bars on six frameworks: square fret, octagons and squares, hexagons, diagonal, interlocking frames and [ice-ray](/chinese-lattice/ice-ray/). Set the bar width and how many cells fit in a repeat, nest up to three frames inside each opening, choose a solid frame or an open edge, then download a seamless repeat, a panel or a printable PDF.

items.caption: Ice-ray with one nested frame, in a solid frame
Octagons and squares, two frames deep
A finer square fret, three cells to a repeat
Interlocking frames in thin bars, with an open edge
Finer ice, with no nested frames

body.text: Each framework is a set of tiles that fill the plane, and a bar is where two tiles meet. Every opening is its tile moved in by half a bar width, so corners, crossings and T-joints are mitered cleanly at any angle, and because the tiles themselves repeat, a bar leaving one side of the repeat comes back in at exactly the same place on the other. Nested frames sit a gap inside the opening and are tied to the frame outside by short bars, so a cut-out lattice holds together.

Ice-ray, 冰裂纹 in Chinese, imitates ice cracking on a pond, so it has no regular grid. Here the ice is broken from points scattered on a surface that wraps around at its edges: each piece is the area nearest one point, and some pieces are cracked once or twice more by a straight cut. The cracks look random, but the repeat still meets its neighbors without a seam. Change the seed to crack it again; the maker remembers your last seed in this browser.

Sorting lattice by its framework, and building richer designs by nesting frames, follows Daniel Sheets Dye's A Grammar of Chinese Lattice (1937), listed in the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/). The designs are constructed from their geometry, not copied from the book's figures. Dye's group labels are descriptions, not traditional names, so the frameworks here have plain names, with the Chinese name given only for ice-ray.

title: Kaleidoscopes you can turn
summary: A new kaleidoscope maker puts beads, glass or one of this site's patterns between two, three or four mirrors, and turns it live with a dial. The three- and four-mirror cells repeat without end.

body.text: The new [kaleidoscope maker](/kaleidoscopes/) puts a picture between mirrors and lets you turn it. Drag the dial, or the slider beside it, and the source spins inside its mirror cell while every reflection follows at once. When you let go, the angle goes into the link, so a shared link, the SVG and PNG, and the printable PDF all show the picture you stopped on. A spin button turns it on its own, and stays off when your device asks for reduced motion.

There are five mirror systems. [Two mirrors](/kaleidoscopes/two-mirror/) at an angle make a round picture of 3 to 12 segments, like the kaleidoscope David Brewster patented in 1817. Three mirrors in a [60-60-60](/kaleidoscopes/60-60-60/), [45-45-90](/kaleidoscopes/45-45-90/) or [30-60-90](/kaleidoscopes/30-60-90/) triangle, or four in a [square](/kaleidoscopes/square/), are the classic cells whose reflections fit together without end, so those come with a seamless repeat to tile across any area.

In the cell you can scatter beads, glass shards or ribbons from a seed, in your palette, or drop in one of this site's own patterns, such as [Truchet tiles](/truchet/) or [sashiko](/sashiko/), which keep their own colors. Zoom and move the source to change which part of it the mirrors catch. The sources behind the mirror angles are on the [acknowledgements](/acknowledgements/) page.

Truchet tiles in a 30-60-90 cell, turned 45°
Sashiko at twice the size, in a 45-45-90 cell
Ribbons in a square of four mirrors

title: Seamless wave patterns, from sine to Lissajous
summary: A new maker draws rows of sine, tangent, square and other waves, moiré and Lissajous figures, as lines or filled bands, in a repeat whose edges always meet.

body.text: The new [wave pattern maker](/waves/) draws rows of waves from ten functions: sine, cosine, tangent, square, triangle, sawtooth, damped, interference, moiré and [Lissajous figures](/waves/lissajous/). Draw them as lines or as filled bands, add a second wave on top, then download a seamless SVG or PNG, or print a PDF at true size.

items.caption: Tangent branches, cut before they run off
Lissajous figures tracing 3:4, slipping row by row
A sine wave carrying a faster one, drifting down the repeat

body.text: Every setting that could break the join counts in whole waves. A repeat holds a whole number of waves across, a second wave adds a whole number of its own, and drift slips the phase by whole waves from top to bottom, so the right edge meets the left and the bottom meets the top. A tangent runs off to infinity, so each branch is cut where it reaches three times the wave's height.

title: Spiral and cone checkerboards
summary: The checkerboard maker can now wind its grid into a spiral, or lay it over a cone seen from above, in every pattern.

body.text: The [checkerboard maker](/checkerboards/) has a new layout setting. The grid is still the default, and two round layouts join it. A spiral winds the grid around a center, so its rows become arms that curl inward and its boxes shrink as they go while keeping their shape, like the classic spiral checkerboard illusion. A cone shows the grid from above a cone's point: rows become rings of equal depth, and columns become wedges that meet in the middle.

Both work with every pattern, from the standard board to [honeycomb](/checkerboards/hexagon/), [brick](/checkerboards/brick/) and houndstooth. Columns count the boxes around and rows count the rings. A spiral picks how far its arms wind so the colors join up all the way round. If they can't, one seam shows where the circle meets itself, and 24 boxes around always joins up.

items.caption: A honeycomb spiral in three colors

items: Grid, spiral and cone layouts, for every checkerboard pattern
Spiral boxes that keep their shape as they shrink toward the center
Cone rings of equal depth, with wedges that meet at the point
A repeat that sets the round board on a square of its first color, so tiles meet edge to edge
SVG, PNG and a printable PDF with the finished size across and each color's pieces

title: Seamless nature patterns: leaves, flowers, clouds and pebbles
summary: A new maker scatters leaves, flowers, clouds, pebbles, ferns or grass across a tile that repeats without a seam.

body.text: The new [nature pattern maker](/nature-patterns/) scatters leaves, flowers, clouds, pebbles, ferns or grass across a square tile that repeats without a seam. Each motif is drawn from simple curves, so no two leaves or [pebbles](/nature-patterns/rocks/) are quite alike, and anything that crosses an edge comes back in on the opposite side.

items: Six motifs: leaves, flowers, clouds, pebbles, ferns and grass, each with its own page

Any palette from the library, or your own colors

title: Endless Patterns now speaks Italian and Dutch
summary: The whole site, with every generated instruction and PDF, is now in Italian and Dutch as well.

body.text: Every page, cutting list, row instruction and PDF is now available in [Italiano](/it/) and [Nederlands](/nl/), alongside English, Spanish, French, German and Brazilian Portuguese. Use the language links at the top of any page to switch.

There are three kinds of puzzle and four pencil games, including [ultimate tic-tac-toe](/paper-puzzles/ultimate-tic-tac-toe/), alongside our [mazes](/mazes/).

Old needlepoint links from the cross-stitch page open on the new page.

summary: Pick a crochet stitch and a square size to get the whole pattern: materials, foundation chain, every row, an edging, and finishing.

body.text: Each stitch in the [knitting library](/knitting/) now gives you a complete pattern for a square, such as a dishcloth or an afghan square, instead of only the rows that repeat. Pick 6, 8, 10 or 12 inches, enter your gauge, and the pattern is written for those numbers.

title: Draw true girih and geometric star patterns
summary: Build a repeating patch from the five girih tiles, or a star pattern on regular polygons, then download a seamless repeat, a stencil, a wall panel and a printable PDF.

body.text: The [geometric stars and girih maker](/girih/) comes from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Its 10-fold option uses the five girih tiles: decagon, pentagon, bowtie, rhombus and elongated hexagon. Every edge is the same length, and lines cross each edge's midpoint at 72 and 108 degrees.

body.text: Only the 10-fold option is called girih. The 4, 6, 8 and 12-fold options are geometric star patterns on regular polygons. An 8, 10 or 12-fold star can't give a whole repeating pattern that symmetry, so the tool lists the star's rotation and the pattern's separately. The girih patch came from a computer search and isn't copied from any building.

body.text: The [mandala maker](/mandalas/) generates geometric radial designs from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Pick 6 to 24 folds of symmetry, 2 to 8 rings, and the motifs each ring may use: petals, arcs, dots, scallops, diamonds or triangles.

title: Design a stained glass panel and print its cutting templates
summary: Choose a design, size, came and colors, then print numbered true-size templates with the came allowance already applied.

body.text: The [stained glass pattern maker](/stained-glass/) is a new tool from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Choose one of four original designs, set the panel size and your came, and pick four glass colors.

items.caption: The numbered key for a border and center

items: A PDF with a numbered key and true-size templates, with the came allowance applied and a 1 inch check square on every template sheet
Pieces too big for a page tiled over taped sheets, and listed as such
A rough glass estimate for each color, including a stated 30% waste allowance
A panel preview as SVG or PNG

body.text: Strict about what can be cut

A score only runs straight from edge to edge, so every piece has straight sides and no inside corners. No corner is under 30 degrees, cut glass is at least 3/4" wide, and long pieces are split. If a design breaks a rule at your size, the tool lowers the detail and tells you. These limits are cautious guidance, not a guarantee, and the estimates are rough, so verify with your came and your supplier.

title: Make a Celtic knot for a laser, a stencil or a coloring page
summary: Build an interlaced knot on a grid, add breaks, and download a cut file, a tattoo stencil, a coloring page, a PNG or a printable PDF.

body.text: The [Celtic knot maker](/celtic-knots/) is a new tool from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Pick a grid size and a break pattern, and it traces the strands into closed loops that go over and under in turn.

Mirrored, rotated and fixed patterns are symmetric. You can give each strand its own color, and the page tells you how many strands your design has.

title: Print a true-size sashiko stitch guide
summary: Choose a geometric motif, a grid size and a panel size, then print a true-size guide with gaps laid out at the crossings.

body.text: The [sashiko stitch guide maker](/sashiko/) draws geometric motifs as dashed stitch lines, ready to print and transfer to your cloth. Choose asanoha, seigaiha, shippo, kikko, kagome or a simple grid, then set the grid size, stitch length, panel size and colors.

items: A true-size PDF, tiled across letter sheets when the panel is larger than one, with a 1 inch check square on each sheet
Stitches centered on each line, so gaps fall at the crossings and stitches don't cross there
An SVG and PNG of the panel in your cloth and thread colors
A rough stitch count and thread estimate

body.text: Sashiko is a Japanese stitching tradition with its own teachers and many ways of working. This tool only draws line guides, and it makes no claims about where a motif comes from. The stitch length and gap are a starting point, so adjust them to your thread, cloth and hand.

title: Make a tessellation in any of the 17 wallpaper groups
summary: Choose a motif, a wallpaper group and your colors, then download a seamless repeat, a tile layout and a printable PDF.

body.text: The [tessellation maker](/tessellations/) is a new tool from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Pick a motif, choose one of the 17 wallpaper groups, and set three colors.

items: A seamless repeat, as SVG or PNG
A tile layout, as SVG or PNG, that marks each repeat and one tile
A printable PDF with the layout, the group's symmetry and one repeat

body.text: The five hexagonal groups have no square repeat. Their smallest upright rectangle is about 1.73 times as tall as it is wide, so that's the shape of the file you download. Tests check each group's rotations, mirrors and glides, and that every repeat meets itself at its edges.

title: Make a printable cross-stitch or needlepoint chart
summary: Choose or draw a motif, set your fabric count and colors, and get a symbol chart, stitch counts, a rough thread estimate and the finished size.

body.text: The [cross-stitch and needlepoint maker](/cross-stitch/) is new in the [pattern library](/patterns/). Start from a motif or draw your own on the grid, then choose your colors and fabric count.

body.text: Colors are plain colors you choose, not matched to any thread brand, so pick the closest thread you have. The motifs were drawn for this site.

body.text: The [tartan and plaid maker](/tartans/) is the first new tool from the [pattern library](/patterns/). Choose thread colors and counts, mirror them if you like, and see the cloth woven in 2/2 twill.

body.text: The presets are invented for this site. Some tartans are restricted or belong to a family or organization, so named historic tartans will be added only with documented sources.

title: Endless Patterns now speaks five languages
summary: The site is now in English, Spanish, French, German and Brazilian Portuguese, with colors that shift a little for each.

body.text: Every page, cutting list, row instruction and PDF is now available in [Español](/es/), [Français](/fr/), [Deutsch](/de/) and [Português](/pt/). Use the language links at the top of any page to switch.
Each language gets a subtle shift in the site's colors and default palette, loosely inspired by a flag commonly associated with it. Each sample below opens in that language.

These translations are a first draft and haven't been reviewed by crafters yet. Block and stitch names stay in English, measurements stay in inches and yards, and needle and hook sizes use US numbering. Crochet uses local abbreviations, with the US term in parentheses.

title: A blog and changelog for what's new
summary: New features now get a post with samples you can open and change, and every update goes in the changelog.

body.text: Endless Patterns now has this blog and a [changelog](/changelog/). The changelog is the short list of what changed and when. Blog posts are for bigger additions, with examples you can try.
